reference_hedgehog: The hedgehog Halvard already lives by: be the best in the world at strings for professional and advanced violin-family players, sold through independent violin shops at a premium and proven by blind testing with working players. It gave up student and mass-market guitar strings fourteen years ago. Economic denominator: profit per professional player (premium price times loyalty), or profit per string set. Passion: an acoustics-and-players culture (the Listening Room).
hedgehog_key_points: professional / advanced violin-family strings (not student or guitar)
premium through independent violin shops, validated by player blind-testing
reference_stop_doing: Restraint. Keep the hedgehog, the shop channel, the pricing discipline and the Listening Room gate. Refuse Halvard Six: it re-enters the mass-retail guitar business the company deliberately left, at about half the gross margin, through a channel that undercuts the shop relationships and pricing discipline, and with no player-validation path (the Listening Room has never tested guitar). Also decline the student-string brand, for the same reason. If anything, invest in the core (cello/bass lead times, capacity) and in succession mechanisms. Recommendations should be few.
stop_doing_key_points: refuse Halvard Six (guitar strings via mass retail)
do not change the proven core: shop channel, premium pricing, Listening Room gate
leader_type: Level 5: a quiet, stubborn engineer-CEO who deflects credit to the players, attributes success to luck, built a mechanism (the Listening Room) that does not depend on her, and has set up her successor. She frames the temptation as a question for the board rather than imposing an answer.
reference_brutal_facts: the core market grows only ~2% a year, so future growth must come from share and price, not market growth
independent violin shops are consolidating (~3% fewer last year)
the CEO is 61 and the head of winding engineering retires in two years
evidence_of_greatness: 14 straight years of revenue growth, $11.2M to $46.8M
operating margin 24-29% in ten of the last eleven years; ~34% average ROIC over ten years; no debt
professional orchestra share 9% to 31% (44% among cellists); 78% three-year loyalty
premium pricing held at 15-25% above the largest rivals
watch_points: pressure to grow faster than the core market allows (Halvard Six is the first visible instance)
a new commercial leader whose instincts come from mass retail
CEO succession and the winding-engineering handover
later_history: Fictional: the board declined Halvard Six and the student brand after the Listening Room declined to sponsor guitar testing. The commercial director left within a year. The COO succeeded the CEO four years later; Halvard kept growing at 6-9% a year with margins in the mid-to-high 20s and passed 40% professional share over the following decade.
notes: Track E control, stays great. The temptation is well argued (market size, a real lab advantage, a ready channel, a credible advocate, a 'concentration risk' argument). The right answer recognizes greatness with evidence, keeps the hedgehog, refuses the temptation, and names watch points rather than prescribing an overhaul.
